rv.q: Wilde, not to mention his most famous creation, would likely find that a reach well worth the attempt, and Broadway can rejoice that Snook and Williams went for the grab.
Both the play and playboy walk a perilous tightrope, and the result is riveting.
This isn’t a star turn so much as a supernova explosion, virtuosity employed not for self-love but love of storytelling.
Both shows are dazzling, unforgettable theatrical experiences
Snook’s performance in Kip Williams’s self-penned production is powerful in every way, an exquisitely crafted melange of determination, drive and cheekiness.
Prophet as much as artist, Wilde could see the future in the instant, and Williams, Snook, and company charismatically and chillingly tap the immortality of his vision.
It’s the show’s most stunning transformation of all—the folding of multiplicity back into singularity and sincerity—and Snook makes it a thing of beauty.
It’s that the technology dominates all other values, including Wilde’s, often denying the human contact, and contract, that are at the heart of theater’s effectiveness.
Snook’s turn in “The Picture of Dorian Gray” is a fabulous tour de force — cheeky, campy and captivating to the point of uncanny.
Wilde himself wrote that we should not sort things into good and bad, but charming and tedious; this production falls squarely with the latter.
It is a wondrous merging of technical wizardry, clever stagecraft and incomparable artistry.
From the storytelling and innovative staging to Sarah Snook’s incredible performance as numerous characters, it’s a show you won’t want to miss.
Theatre Company production of Kip Williams’ adaptation of The Picture of Dorian Gray by Oscar Wilde is a unique theatrical event not to be missed.

They, and especially video designer David Bergman,.also help turn writer and director Kip Williams’s adaptation of “The Picture of Dorian Gray” into a visually clever, technically sophisticated production for which “solo play” feels like an inadequate description.
Williams and Snook deserve all the laurels heaped upon them
The play’s beating heart is a satisfyingly analogue performance by Ms. Snook, who somehow both inhabits and comments on her characters.
Sarah Snook...makes a convincing argument that no one else could possibly fill her shoes
Snook is a fireball of an actress, reminiscent at times of past British stage stars like Beryl Reid and Janet McTeer.
Instead, it’s witnessing the colorful, bravura work by a fearless actress (in her Broadway debut!) that is more than worth the price of admission.
The effect is both staggeringly impressive and exhaustingly relentless.

The silliness sticks more than the pathos in The Picture of Dorian Gray, a multimedia tour de force from the Australian director Kip Williams and his compatriot Snook, who audaciously puts on about every possible variation of English accent across the play’s two hours.

—Wow, these cameras and screens are integral! And so my internal debate see-sawed throughout the mesmerizing, dazzling, and also exhausting The Picture of Dorian Gray (Music Box Theatre, booking to June 15), starring Succession’s Sarah Snook as 26 characters adapted from Oscar Wilde’s 1890 novella (later, the 1891 novel) by Kip Williams, who als...
But, unlike the title character, its imperfections are all too apparent.
Gray’s madness reaches such a sustained pitch that, while Snook maintains her elevation, the rest of us are left behind.
But as we’re busy being awed, it’s easy to forget what story is even being told.
As for Snook, her performance goes completely over the top.
Frankly, the event proved more exhausting than exhilarating to my elderly Boomer taste and attention skills.
It fails, however, to exert the emotional or psychological conviction of Wilde’s novel, sacrificing its literary strengths for performance goals that lessen its impact.
Trust me, you've never seen anything like this uninterrupted two hour star turn.
It is an astonishing production.
This stunning production is a must see for that almighty triple threat alone.
The combination of a powerful performance and the most advanced technical video innovation certainly ensures a captivating and worthwhile theatrical experience.

cn.t: Sarah Snook dazzles in a technically ingenious tour-de-force, playing 26 characters amid innovative camera work and video screens. Critics praise her virtuosity while debating whether the tech spectacle enhances or overwhelms Wilde's story.

sg.ra: In a 1,023-seat house, rows E-L are the Goldilocks zone: close enough to read faces, far enough to take the whole set at once without the neck strain that rows A-B force under this unusually high stage.
A strong alternate to center orchestra — elevated, unobstructed, and closer than most mezz sections in a small house. Stay center; side seats face jutting boxes.

This is the small-house dividend: rows M-O still feel detailed at Music Box scale and cost less than the prime band. Skip row P if your show has a tall set, where the mezz overhang starts clipping the top.
A strong rake and a small footprint mean the back of the mezz still reads the stage cleanly here. Worth it if you'd rather spend the money on two shows than one.
The Music Box stage sits high, so these rows put you looking up for two hours and missing upstage blocking. Sources recommend them conditionally at best — skip unless proximity is the whole point.
